levels.title: Odds and Evens
levels.story: Fenn flips a coin on the fence post. "Heads, I go to market. Tails, I mend the fence." Then Fenn looks at the clouds. "But for rain I don't flip a coin. I count. After a hundred mornings of notes, I can do better than 'who knows'."

everyday.scene: A weather app says '70% chance of rain'. It does not know what will happen. It says that in days like this one, it rained about 7 times out of every 10.
everyday.question: What does a probability tell you?
everyday.answer: How often something happens in situations like this one. Many machine learning models give their answers as probabilities, and then pick the most likely one.

lessons.title: Probability by counting
text: A probability is a number from 0 to 1. Zero means never and 1 means always. One way to estimate it is by counting: the number of days it happened divided by the number of days you looked at.
The table covers 100 mornings. Rain followed on 35 of them, so the chance of rain is 35 out of 100, or 0.35. The chances of all the possible outcomes add up to 1, so no rain is 0.65.

lessons.title: Given and both
text: A conditional probability is a chance among a narrowed group. The chance of rain given a cloudy morning looks only at the 50 cloudy mornings, and 30 of them had rain. That is 30 out of 50, or 0.6.

Two events are independent when one tells you nothing about the other. Then the chance of both is the two chances multiplied. If two fields each have a 0.35 chance of rain, independently, both get rain with chance 0.35 x 0.35 = 0.1225.

predict.prompt: Of the 50 cloudy mornings, 30 had rain. What is the chance of rain given a cloudy morning?

lessons.title: A model gives chances
text: A probabilistic model turns clues into chances and then picks the most likely answer. Here, a cloudy morning gives 0.6 for rain, so the model would say rain.
Counting is only as good as the sample. If a coin lands heads 3 times out of 3, counting says the chance is 1. With only three flips, that is too confident. More data makes the estimate steadier.

fieldNotes.title: Conditional chances
fieldNotes.text: A conditional probability is the probability of an event given that another event has already happened, for example the chance of rain given a cloudy sky.

fieldNotes.title: Forecasts are chances
fieldNotes.text: A forecast of a 70 percent chance of rain gives the probability that a given spot gets measurable rain. It is not a promise that it will rain.

source.title: National Weather Service: Explaining Probability of Precipitation

mistake.title: Dividing by all the days instead of the group you are given

levels.title: Count the Clues
levels.story: The farm's inbox is filling up. Some notes are orders, and some are junk. Fenn reads one aloud: "'Eggs, free delivery.' Hmm. 'Eggs' sounds like an order, and 'free' sounds like junk. Which clue wins?"

everyday.scene: A spam filter sees an email with the words 'winner', 'free' and 'click'. Each word on its own is only a small hint, but together they add up.
everyday.question: How can a computer weigh several small clues at once?
everyday.answer: It multiplies how common each clue is in each class, starting from how common the class is. Whichever class scores higher wins. That method is called naive Bayes.

lessons.title: Start with how common
text: Naive Bayes starts from the prior: how common each class is. Of 20 past notes, 12 were Orders and 8 were Junk, so the priors are 0.6 and 0.4.
Then it asks, for each word, how often that word shows up in notes of each class. The table counts the notes containing each word. 'Eggs' is in 9 of the 12 Orders and 1 of the 8 Junk notes.

lessons.title: Multiply the clues
text: The 'naive' part is a simple assumption: given the class, each word is independent of the others. Then you can multiply. For a note with 'eggs' and 'free', the Order score is 0.6 x 9/12 x 2/12 = 0.075, and the Junk score is 0.4 x 1/8 x 6/8 = 0.0375.
Divide each score by the total to get chances. Order gets two thirds. The assumption is rarely true, since words come in pairs, but the method often works well anyway.

predict.prompt: Order scores 0.075 and Junk scores 0.0375. What chance does Order get?

lessons.title: The zero problem
text: Suppose the word 'pigeon' has never appeared in an Order. Then its Order count is 0, and multiplying by 0 wipes out the whole score, however strong the other clues are.

text.text: The fix is smoothing: add 1 to each count and 2 to each total, as if every word had been seen once with and once without. (The general rule adds 1 to each count and the number of possible outcomes to the total, which is 2 here.) For 'eggs' and 'pigeon', Order scores 3/98 and Junk scores 2/125, and Order wins with about 0.66.

references.title: Speech and Language Processing, chapter 4: Naive Bayes, Text Classification, and Sentiment

fieldNotes.title: Why 'naive'
fieldNotes.text: Naive Bayes classifiers assume that the features are conditionally independent given the class. The page calls this assumption highly unrealistic, which is where the name 'naive' comes from.

fieldNotes.title: Spam and text
fieldNotes.text: Naive Bayes is well known for document classification and spam filtering, and it can be extremely fast compared with more sophisticated methods.
